title: Python Tuple Methods: count() and index()
learningObjectives: Explain the two built-in methods available on Python tuples.
Use count() to count occurrences of a specified value.
Use index() to find the first occurrence of a value.
Use the optional start and end bounds supported by index().
Handle a missing value safely because index() raises ValueError when no match exists.

understand.concept: Python tuples provide two built-in methods: count(value) returns how many times a value occurs, and index(value, start, end) returns the position of its first occurrence within the optional search bounds. Tuples are immutable, so these methods inspect values without changing the tuple. index() raises ValueError when the requested value is not found in the selected range.
understand.whyItMatters: Tuple methods let a program inspect immutable records without converting them to lists. Knowing the difference between counting matches and locating the first match prevents incorrect assumptions about duplicates.
understand.analogy: count() tells you how many copies of a label appear in a row of numbered boxes; index() tells you the position of the first matching label.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not capture Python's zero-based indexing or the optional half-open search bounds.
understand.summary: Use count() for frequency and index() for the first matching position; handle ValueError when a searched value may be absent.

explain.narrative:
## count(value)
`tuple.count(value)` returns the number of matching elements. It returns zero when the value does not occur.

## index(value, start, end)
`tuple.index(value)` returns the first matching index. Optional `start` and `end` values restrict the search; the end position is excluded, following Python's normal slicing convention.

## Errors and immutability
If the value is not found in the selected range, `index()` raises `ValueError`. Neither method changes the tuple.

examples.title: Count repeated values
examples.explanation: count returns the number of occurrences of the requested value.

examples.title: Count a value that is absent
examples.explanation: count returns zero rather than raising an exception when no matching value exists.

examples.title: Find the first matching index
examples.explanation: index returns the position of the first occurrence, using zero-based indexing.

examples.title: Search from a starting position
examples.explanation: The start argument skips earlier positions and finds the next matching value.

examples.title: Handle a value that is not found
examples.explanation: index raises ValueError when no match is found in the requested search range.

practise.guidedTask: Create a tuple containing repeated values. Use count() to report a frequency, then use index() to find the first occurrence and compare it with a search that starts later.
practise.independentTask: Build a small tuple-based record check that counts a status value, locates its first occurrence and reports a clear message when a requested value is absent.
hints: Use count(value) to count all matches.
Remember that tuple indexes start at zero.
index(value, start, end) searches a bounded range.
The end argument is excluded from the search.
Catch ValueError when index() may not find a match.
practise.challenge: Write a reusable helper that returns both the count and first index of a value, using None for the index when the value is absent without modifying the original tuple.
validationCriteria: All examples use tuple methods correctly.
The index result is zero-based and identifies the first match in the selected range.
